newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian OLOs unmoved by shaky coalition partner.
newsitem.headline: Belgian OLOs unmoved by shaky coalition partner.

text.p: The tainted credibility of one of the four partners in Belgium's centre-left coalition has so far failed to move the market in Belgian government bonds (OLOs), but left something of a mark on the franc.
OLO futures and cash prices eased on Monday, but dealers said this was a markdown after recent gains, with players using a market holiday in the U.S. for some profit-taking.

The outlook was for cautious trading until the second half of the week when fresh U.S. and German indicators could stir up business. Before then there could be some spread-widening versus Bunds in the run-up to Tuesday's regular OLO auction.

To offset the softness of the franc, short-term interest rates have spiked higher. Most notably, one-week repo rates are at 3.12/15 percent, up from 3.11/14 on Friday. They began moving away from the central bank's central rate of three percent as the franc slipped when the PS news broke about a month ago.

Dealers said, however, the fundamental backdrop for OLOs was sound and politically most investors -- the bulk conservative domestics -- would not worry about the scandals until the government of Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene was threatened.
"Dehaene will not be moved," said a trader. As long as there was no threat of elections, OLO holders would sit tight.

A replacement of the socialists by francophone liberals would not move the market, dealers said, since the government would continue to function and its drive towards EMU, marked by spending cuts and a reform of social security, would not be interrupted. "Dehaene will never allow elections," said one.

"Dehaene is one of the few who can keep Belgium on course for EMU...actually, it is disgraceful the government continues with such a partner, but (the single currency) is more important (for it) than these political episodes," said another.
Conservative investors were also shrugging off advice from
some houses to switch into Bunds from OLOs.
"The consensus view is that (in yield terms) Belgium should trade above Germany in most maturities with a 10-year spread at around 10-15 basis points," JP Morgan in Brussels said.
The spread was at three basis points at 1635 GMT.

"(A) lack of potential for outperformance, and the dearness of the Belgian curve, will lead more diversification away from OLOs. In addition, the political situation in Belgium still looks shaky: support for the government is very low, social unrest over pensions, plant closures and work flexibility is picking up and there are potentially more scandals to come. Sell Belgian assets into German ones," it said.
But more fundamentally-oriented players said the country's strong current account surplus, subdued inflation, a recovering economy and good EMU prospects meant OLOs should not be sold.
The EMU prospects for Belgium were underlined earlier on Monday by EU finance ministers, who praised the government's 1997-2000 convergence plan as "credible and adequate."

One trader said, however, OLOs were not a buy either. "I would buy in a correction only." Another said this view would rob OLOs of much potential, definitely before tomorrow's auction, but also with a view to nervousness about the course of U.S. rates. -- Nieck Ammerlaan, Brussels Newsroom +32 2 287 6816, Fax +32 2 230 7710
